title: The fraud hunters' ledger: two dead citizens, no fraud arrests from the surge, and a $420 million markup on a prison
dek: Analysis. The administration justified flooding Minneapolis with federal agents by pointing at Minnesota's fraud scandals. Ten months on, the surge's arrest data, the evidence still withheld in two killings and ICE's own real estate record show who was watching whom.
body:
*Analysis.* On Friday morning the Treasury secretary, the FBI director and the head of Medicare and Medicaid stood in a police station in St. Cloud, Minnesota, under a banner for the vice president's fraud task force, to announce that four home-care and autism-therapy providers had been charged with stealing from Medicaid [1][2][3]. The vice president himself had canceled the night before [1]. Scott Bessent told the room that fraud was all over the state and that Governor Tim Walz's administration had turned a blind eye to it [1]. Then a local reporter asked about the $420 million the federal government had paid above the asking price for a prison three hours west, and Bessent said he did not know anything about it and that such questions were a waste of the task force's time [2][3].

It was a small moment, and it was the whole year in miniature. Since December the administration has treated Minnesota as a crime scene: a state so riddled with fraud that it justified the largest immigration operation in the country's history, a sustained attack on its governor, threats to its Medicaid funding and, now, a roadshow of cabinet officers days before an election [1][2][4][5]. The record of what the federal government actually did in Minnesota over those ten months is now long enough to read on its own terms. It includes two dead American citizens, an arrest ledger that does not match the stated purpose, evidence withheld from state prosecutors and a real estate bill that the government's own auditor describes with the word the administration reserves for other people. (The sale itself is laid out in [The Watch's report on the Appleton deal](https://bboldt86.github.io/lanscape-navigator/news/#/a/2026-10-31-ice-paid-495-million-for-appleton-prison-offered-for-75).)

## The pretext

The surge was sold on fraud. The administration cited the state's social-services scandals, above all the pandemic meals scheme known as Feeding Our Future, to justify sending thousands of federal immigration agents into Minnesota last winter, and the president singled out Somali immigrants, calling them garbage [1][4]. Operation Metro Surge was announced on December 4, expanded on January 6 to 2,000 agents, and by late January involved at least 2,000 ICE officers and 1,000 Customs and Border Protection officers, according to a Justice Department lawyer's testimony [4]. The White House said it produced at least 4,000 arrests [5].

The data released since tell a different story about who was arrested. A CBS News analysis of government records obtained by the Deportation Data Project counted about 3,800 arrests between December 1 and March 10; 24 percent of the people taken had a criminal conviction, 13 percent had a pending charge of some kind and 63 percent were arrested for immigration violations alone [6]. The largest group was Ecuadorian [6]. Somali nationals, the stated target, were under 3 percent, about 106 people, and none had any tie to the fraud under investigation [6][4]. No one arrested in the operation was charged with fraud [1].

The federal courts in Minnesota kept their own count. Chief Judge Patrick Schiltz found in late January that ICE had violated at least 96 court orders in the state since the start of the year, and Judge Jerry Blackwell said the overwhelming majority of the ICE cases in front of him involved people lawfully in the country [4]. On February 12, border czar Tom Homan announced the operation was ending and said he did not want to see any more bloodshed [5]. Attorney General Keith Ellison told a Senate committee it had been retribution for how the state votes; Representative Tom Emmer, the House Republican whip, blamed the clashes on sanctuary policies [5].

## Two citizens, ten months, no charges

The bloodshed Homan referred to had names. Renee Good, 37, a mother of three, was shot on January 7 by an ICE officer as she left a protest in Minneapolis; bystander video shows her in the driver's seat, honking, as masked officers order her out, and the officer in front of the car firing through the windshield and then twice more from about an arm's length away, according to an Associated Press analysis [7]. The officer was Jonathan Ross [8]. Federal officials said he fired in self-defense and that Good had weaponized her car; local officials say the video contradicts that, and DHS has maintained its account [7][8].

Alex Pretti, also 37, an intensive-care nurse at the VA, was killed on January 24 while recording Border Patrol agents on Nicollet Avenue [9][10]. ABC News reconstructed the three minutes from six verified videos: Pretti holding up his phone; an officer pepper-spraying him as he raises a hand; the officer dragging him into the street by his hood; several officers pinning him while one punches him; an officer removing a handgun from his waistband; and then ten shots in under five seconds, the first fired about one second after the gun was taken [9]. Pretti had a permit to carry [4]. That day DHS Secretary Kristi Noem said he had come to the scene to kill law enforcement [9]. A former acting DHS intelligence chief who reviewed the footage for ABC said the videos showed no threatening approach at all [9].

The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division opened an investigation into Pretti's death and declined to open one into Good's, with Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche explaining that the division does not examine every police shooting [10]. Federal prosecutors in Minnesota resigned in protest at how the Good case was handled [4]. State investigators were denied access to both scenes and told there would be no joint investigation into the agents' use of force [4][8][22]. Minnesota and Hennepin County sued in March for the evidence; in July the government began handing some over, and on September 10 the U.S. Attorney's office told Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty that sharing was paused indefinitely "in light of challenges with D.C." [7]. As of last week the state still did not have Good's clothing, the phone of the officer who killed her, a recorded statement from the officer who shot Pretti, the firearms, the casings or the gun taken from Pretti; Good's car sits shrink-wrapped in an FBI warehouse, never examined [7][8]. Justice Department lawyers argue that sharing is within their discretion and have suggested the state has no jurisdiction over federal officers at all [7].

No one has been charged in either death [7]. In the one Metro Surge shooting that has produced charges, the wounding of a Venezuelan man named Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, Moriarty charged ICE agent Christian Castro in May with four counts of assault and one of falsely reporting a crime; DHS itself said two officers had made untruthful statements and put them on leave [4][8][11]. Castro is in a Texas jail, and Governor Greg Abbott has refused to sign the extradition order, saying he will not respond until Minnesota does what is right, a reference to the state's fraud problems [11]. Fraud, in other words, is now the stated reason an agent charged with shooting a man and lying about it will not face a Minnesota court.

The shootings were the extreme. ProPublica has documented 506 U.S. citizens detained by immigration agents during this administration, more than a hundred of them held after agents questioned their citizenship, at least 70 of them children or teenagers, roughly a dozen deported [12][13].

## The ledger

Now the money. KARE 11 reported this week that in May 2025 CoreCivic offered its empty Appleton prison to the state for $75 million, and that in August the Department of Homeland Security paid $495.6 million for it [14][15]. The county assessor values it at $14.75 million [16]. The difference, about $420 million, is larger than the roughly $300 million estimated to have been stolen in Feeding Our Future, the scandal the administration invokes most often [1][15]. CoreCivic says independent appraisers used a cost-based method and the government set the price [15]. The company will also run the building for ICE through 2031 at about $75 million a year [17]. Six days after the sale closed it put $500 million of cash into buying back its own stock [18]. It had given $500,000 to the inaugural committee and spent $1.77 million lobbying on the budget law that funds the purchases [16].

Appleton is not an outlier. The same law gave ICE $45 billion for detention through 2029, against about $3.8 billion in ordinary appropriations for detention facilities in fiscal 2025, and the Government Accountability Office reported in September that ICE spent it without a strategic plan, bought eleven warehouses for $1.07 billion, is now trying to sell seven of them and has written off more than $20 million it cannot recover [19][20]. The GAO's title was "Urgent Planning Needed to Avoid Further Waste of Taxpayer Dollars" [19]. ICE agreed to write a plan by August 2027 [19]. In the same summer the government paid CoreCivic about $2.2 billion for four prisons, including $739 million for a San Diego facility assessed at $160 million [15][16][23].

Nobody has alleged that any of this broke a law. Ellison calls it scamming taxpayers out of almost half a billion dollars and has asked three congressional committees to investigate; the government's auditor calls the wider program waste; CoreCivic calls it the result of the government's assessment process [15][16][19]. The administration's word for it is nothing, because the question is a waste of time [2][3].

## Fraud, by whose definition

The cases announced in St. Cloud are real. Prosecutors in Minnesota have charged more than a hundred people in social-services fraud since 2022, a woman was convicted on October 7 of health care fraud tied to the housing-stabilization program that the Walz administration shut down last year, and one of Friday's defendants is expected to plead guilty in a $14 million Medicaid case [1]. The core allegation in nearly all of them is simple: billing a public program for services that were not provided [2].

The administration has a looser standard for itself. Mehmet Oz on Friday presented the mass removal of Minnesota Medicaid providers as evidence of fraud; the Minnesota Reformer reports that the state's Department of Human Services disenrolled 60 percent of providers in 13 high-risk services under a rushed federal deadline, often for paperwork reasons, that the state asked Oz in writing to stop counting administrative actions as fraud, and that the federal government has meanwhile threatened to cut $2 billion a year from the state's Medicaid funding [2]. Walz's office called the St. Cloud event a political spectacle staged days before an election [1].

Set the two standards side by side. A home-care owner who bills for a client who is away at a funeral is a fraudster [2], and the FBI director holds up a placard from a convicted defendant's website [1]. A federal agency that pays six and a half times the asking price for a building, with no public appraisal, to a donor, and then will not answer for it, is conducting an assessment process [15][16]. An agent who shoots a man and lies about it is shielded from a Minnesota courtroom in the name of fraud [11]. Two citizens are dead in the street and the evidence is in a federal warehouse marked discretionary [7][8].

## What to watch

- **The county attorney's election.** Moriarty is not running again; Tuesday's race between Cedrick Frazier, whose yard signs read "Prosecute ICE," and Anders Folk, a former interim U.S. attorney, may decide who makes the charging decision in the Good and Pretti cases [21].
- **The evidence fight.** State prosecutors have asked a federal judge again to order the handover; the Justice Department's reply argues it can decline [7].
- **Castro's extradition.** Minnesota has sued Texas; Abbott has not answered the suit [11].
- **Appleton's first detainees,** and whether Congress, which Ellison has asked to investigate, asks DHS for the appraisal [16][17].
